web_title: 5. Management Promises, Plant Timelines & the KPIs That Matter
question: Which numbers should you track, and have the promises made so far been kept on time?

epigraph.quote: The ESOP is not an expense, it is not a payout, company doesn't have to pay anything, company does not lose any money, there's nothing.
epigraph.author: Shazad Rustomji, Chairman, CEO and Managing Director, Q2 and H1 FY27 earnings call, 19 November 2026 [36]

web_blocks.html: A management team makes promises in two currencies, turnover and dates. This chapter tracks both. It starts with six numbers you can check each quarter, then audits every dated promise the filings let us verify. The November 2026 disclosures, monitoring agency reports, and earnings call transcript turned earlier open questions into hard scorecards [36][37][38].
The scorecard uses only what exchange filings, monitoring reports, and earnings transcripts state. Where management gave no formal target, the table says so rather than inventing one.

web_blocks.takeaway: Overall KPI health deteriorated to fail in November 2026: Khalapur finally started 334 days late, while Bhilwara and Mambattu both slipped again into FY28 with cost overruns, core margin dropped below 10%, and operating cash flow relapsed to −₹39.17 crore [36][37][38].

web_blocks.html: Reading the six rows together shows why top-line growth alone cannot carry the thesis. First-half revenue rose 19.18% year on year, yet core operating margins narrowed, operating cash flow swung back to a deep outflow, and neither flagship growth plant will contribute a rupee of sales in FY27 [36][37][38].

web_blocks.title: What management promised, and what the record shows

web_blocks.html: The record now spans four dated checkpoints: the January 2025 IPO prospectus, the October 2025 and August 2026 calls, and the November 2026 quarterly filings and monitoring agency reports. Every verifiable claim is tested below.

web_blocks.caption: Promise audit: dated claims from the IPO prospectus, October 2025, August 2026, and November 2026 disclosures [1][8][9][10][36][37][38]

web_blocks.takeaway: One annual revenue promise was kept (FY26), Khalapur finally started 334 days behind its IPO date, and both Bhilwara R-32 and Mambattu broke their FY27 commissioning and revenue timelines while incurring cost overruns and requiring fresh capital [36][37][38].

web_blocks.html: The monitoring agency reports closed the disclosure gap flagged in the prior draft. CARE Ratings’ 14 November 2026 IPO report documented that the original prospectus completion dates for both Khalapur (₹29.16 crore revised to ₹25.75 crore) and Mambattu (₹21.17 crore) were 30 October 2025 [37]. Shareholders extended those dates on 3 June 2026 to 30 June 2026 and 30 August 2026, and both plants breached even the extended deadlines without further shareholder approval [37].

web_blocks.title: The plant timelines, one at a time

web_blocks.html: The Bhilwara R-32 plant has now established a clear pattern of slippage. Promised for July 2026 in October 2025 [10], scheduled for 30 August 2026 in the Rights Issue letter of offer, and moved to end-December 2026 in August 2026 [9], the project was formally revised in Infomerics’ 14 November 2026 monitoring report to 30 March 2027—a seven-month rights-issue delay [38]. On the 19 November 2026 call, Chairman, CEO and Managing Director Shazad Rustomji stated verbatim: “We expect to have all trials completed by March. And from April, we should have the production as per the current plans” [36]. He blamed late funding receipt in April 2026, monsoon clayey-soil foundation rework, and statutory certification design changes [36].

Cost discipline slipped alongside the schedule. On the same call, Rustomji confirmed the budget increase verbatim: “In this Bhilwara project, about 40 crores is overrun, which is currently internally funded. The overrun is on basis of having the iso tank containers. The company has purchased over 90 containers and additional equipment” [36]. FY27 R-32 revenue fell from the earlier ₹250 crore expectation to zero. Meanwhile, Khalapur helium (1,200 MTPA) began commercial operations on 21 September 2026 (recorded as completed 29 September in CARE Ratings’ log—334 days late), while Mambattu slipped past end-2026 to January 2027 or Q1 FY28 after an acreage-wide redesign nearly doubled its cost scope, likewise delivering zero FY27 sales [36][37].

web_blocks.title: The revenue guidance, put in numbers

web_blocks.html: Even with zero FY27 revenue from Bhilwara or Mambattu, Rustomji reaffirmed Stallion’s internal ₹560 crore FY27 revenue target on the 19 November 2026 call, explaining that “obviously we will not have 32, so the figure of 500 crores as the growth would be in effect. However, wanting to ensure and make sure that whatever we speak becomes a form of a commitment and not loose talk, our target had moved up to 560 crores itself internally” [36]. Having delivered ₹257.48 crore in H1 FY27 (+19.18% YoY), Stallion now requires ₹302.52 crore in H2 FY27 (+41% over H2 FY26’s ₹214.64 crore) from existing operations and early Khalapur helium volumes [1][36].

For FY28, management scaled back from its August remark of “Exceeding 1100 crores” [9] to roughly ₹1,000 crore, assuming ₹350 to ₹400 crore from 7,000 tonnes of first-year Bhilwara R-32 output alongside roughly ₹600 crore from core lines [36]. Management also voiced an ambition of ₹3,000 crore (or “safely” ₹2,500 crore) by FY30—a projection unsupported by any filed capex or funding schedule, especially with HFO construction still awaiting environmental clearance and financing [36].

web_blocks.title: The September 2026 quarter, explained—and what the CEO said on the call

web_blocks.html: The September 2026 quarter posted the lowest operating margin in the ten-quarter Screener series: 2.20% operating margin (₹2.99 crore operating profit excluding other income) and ₹2.45 crore net profit on ₹136.03 crore of revenue, with other income (₹3.34 crore) exceeding operating profit and an effective tax rate of 57.22% [14]. The November 2026 press release and 19 November earnings call finally explained the mechanics—and revealed both an accounting charge and genuine spread compression [36].

On the accounting side, Stallion granted 15,86,505 equity-settled options at ₹10 face-value exercise price (one-year vesting) and booked ₹9.51 crore (₹950.92 lakh) of non-cash Ind AS 102 ESOP expense in Q2 FY27 as a two-quarter catch-up, with roughly ₹4.7 crore per quarter continuing in Q3 and Q4 FY27 (~₹19 crore full-year charge) [36]. Because the ₹3.29 crore quarterly tax charge was levied on roughly ₹15.25 crore of pre-ESOP pre-tax profit (~21.6% effective rate) rather than ₹5.75 crore of reported pre-tax profit, the reported tax ratio jumped to 57.22% [14][36]. Management emphasized Operating EBITDA before ESOP (which includes ₹3.34 crore of other income) of ₹15.84 crore (+0.43% YoY) and Operating PAT before ESOP of ₹11.96 crore (+4.78% YoY) [36]. Yet stripping out both the ESOP charge and non-operating other income leaves core operating profit of just ₹12.50 crore—a 9.19% margin, down about 557 basis points YoY (14.76%) and 896 basis points QoQ (18.15%)—as raw-material costs surged 38.95% YoY on Gulf input inflation, higher freight, and quota-year selling pressure [14][36].

Equally revealing was who spoke on the 19 November 2026 earnings call and how management addressed financial discipline. Per the official BSE transcript cover sheet, no Chief Financial Officer attended or spoke on the call; Chairman, CEO and Managing Director Shazad Rustomji was the sole management representative fielding investor questions on the 57.22% tax rate, the ESOP charge, and negative cash flow [36]. On ESOP accounting, Rustomji told analysts verbatim: “The ESOP is not an expense, it is not a payout, company doesn't have to pay anything, company does not lose any money, there's nothing. It is a provision for accounting provided as per the current and latest standards” [36]. Pressed by an analyst on H1 FY27 operating cash flow turning negative again, Rustomji replied verbatim: “Now basically cash flow is not a true reflection of anything” [36]. On financing the next leg of expansion, he added verbatim: “Either we may raise funds through a QIP preferential or we may raise debentures or we may go down debt. It's not decided yet” [36]. For minority shareholders, dismissing real equity dilution and operating cash conversion—without a CFO present to walk through working capital—is a major governance warning.

web_blocks.company: Olin Corporation (United States, Chlor Alkali Products and Vinyls segment)
web_blocks.region_era: United States, 2022 to 2023, chlor-alkali and vinyls commodity cycle
web_blocks.mechanism: A commodity-spread segment lost profit faster than sales in a single year, as volumes and selling rates fell together. The fourth-quarter margin fell by about two-thirds.
web_blocks.outcome_numbers: Segment income before taxes fell from $1,181.3 million in 2022 to $664.2 million in 2023 on sales of $5,085.0 million and $3,995.1 million, a margin of about 23% falling to about 17% [30]. Fourth-quarter segment earnings fell from $252.3 million on $1,172.8 million of sales to $65.9 million on $906.1 million, a margin of about 21.5% falling to about 7.3% [31].
web_blocks.lesson_for_symbol: Judge a commodity earnings base by its trough margin, not its peak. Stallion’s own EBITDA margin fell from 17.71% to 6.90% in one year [7], and Q2 FY27 showed core operating spreads compressing back below 10% even before ESOP charges [36].

web_blocks.html: This is only half of the Olin case. The annual figure is income before taxes and the quarterly figure is segment earnings, so the two are close rather than identical measures. The filings show how fast a chemical spread can collapse once pricing weakens, even before capacity additions arrive.

web_blocks.title: NARRATOR’S REFLECTION
paragraphs: The first time a plant date moves, it is a note. The second time, it is a pattern. Bhilwara has now moved from July 2026 to August 2026 to December 2026 to April and May 2027, and Mambattu has moved from October 2025 to August 2026 to January 2027 or Q1 FY28—both with cost overruns and zero FY27 revenue [36][37][38]. That is an established execution breakdown.

Watch how management speaks when results disappoint. With no CFO on the 19 November call, the Chairman and CEO dismissed a ₹19 crore annual face-value ESOP program as “not an expense” and declared operating cash flow “not a true reflection of anything” while flagging a third capital raise in two years [36]. Those words tell you exactly how much weight to place on ambitious FY28 and FY30 forecasts.

book_paragraphs: Now let us test the promises. A management team makes promises in two currencies: a number, such as turnover or profit, and a date, such as when a plant will run. Dates are easier to check, because a plant either starts on schedule or it does not. The November 2026 filings, monitoring agency reports, and earnings call transcript turned earlier open questions into hard verdicts.

Start with the one kept promise. In October 2025 management guided FY26 turnover of about 430 crore and profit after tax of about 40 crore. The audited accounts came in at 430.68 crore and 43.84 crore. Give credit where it is due, and then examine what happened to every single plant date that followed.

Bhilwara R-32 has now slipped four times into an unmistakable pattern. Promised within nine months (July 2026) in October 2025, dated August 2026 in the rights issue document, and pushed to December 2026 in August, the project was formally revised in Infomerics’ 14 November 2026 monitoring report to 30 March 2027—a seven-month delay versus the rights issue schedule. On the 19 November earnings call, Chairman and CEO Shazad Rustomji confirmed trials by March, phased production in April, and full stabilization in May 2027. He blamed late rights-issue funding, monsoon clayey soil, and statutory design changes.

Costs slipped right alongside the calendar. On the same call, Rustomji disclosed roughly 40 crore of cost overruns at Bhilwara for over 90 ISO-tank containers and additional equipment, wiping out FY27 R-32 revenue from an earlier 250 crore expectation down to zero. Mambattu followed the exact same script. Originally due in October 2025 in the IPO prospectus, extended by shareholders to August 2026, and promised for end-2026 in August, Mambattu has now slipped to January 2027 or Q1 FY28 with zero FY27 revenue and nearly doubled cost scope after a full site redesign.

Khalapur helium did cross the finish line, commencing commercial operations on 21 September 2026. Even there, CARE Ratings logged formal completion on 29 September 2026—a 334-day delay versus the original IPO prospectus schedule and past the June 2026 shareholder extension, with standalone helium revenue still undisclosed.

Funding promises shifted just as often as plant dates. Promised from internal accruals in October 2025, Bhilwara instead required a 363.93 crore rights issue in February 2026. By November 2026, both IPO and rights-issue pools were virtually exhausted, and Rustomji told analysts management is already weighing a fresh 200 crore raise through a QIP, preferential allotment, debentures, or debt to fund R-32 working capital, project overruns, and future HFO capex.

Set the revenue guidance next to that execution track record. Even with zero FY27 revenue from Bhilwara or Mambattu, Rustomji reaffirmed an internal FY27 target of 560 crore, which demands 302.52 crore in the second half—up 41% over last year’s second half—after 257.48 crore in the first half. For FY28, guidance stepped down from exceeding 1,100 crore to around 1,000 crore, hinging on 7,000 tonnes of first-year Bhilwara R-32 output. Management even floated an FY30 ambition of 2,500 to 3,000 crore despite lacking environmental clearance or funding for its HFO plant. Treat those outer-year projections with deep skepticism until Bhilwara actually runs at commercial yield.

The November 2026 disclosures also decoded the September 2026 quarter’s jarring 2.20% operating margin and 57.22% effective tax rate. Two separate blows landed together. First, Stallion granted 15.87 lakh equity options at 10 rupees face value and booked a 9.51 crore non-cash ESOP charge as a two-quarter catch-up, with roughly 4.7 crore per quarter continuing in Q3 and Q4. Because taxes were levied on roughly 15.25 crore of pre-ESOP profit rather than 5.75 crore of reported pre-tax profit, the reported tax rate spiked above 57%.

Second, strip out both the ESOP charge and 3.34 crore of non-operating other income, and core operating profit still fell to 12.50 crore—a 9.19% margin, down roughly 557 basis points year on year from 14.76% and nearly 900 basis points from June’s 18.15%. Raw-material costs surged nearly 39% on Gulf input inflation, higher freight, and quota-year selling pressure. The September shock was not purely accounting optics; the underlying import-and-blend spread genuinely compressed.

Just as telling was the governance tone on the 19 November call. No Chief Financial Officer attended or spoke on the earnings call, leaving Chairman and CEO Shazad Rustomji as the sole management speaker answering every financial question. On the ESOP program, Rustomji told investors that the ESOP is not an expense, not a payout, and costs the company nothing. Pressed on why H1 FY27 operating cash flow relapsed to negative 39.17 crore, he replied that cash flow is not a true reflection of anything.

Olin Corporation’s chlor-alkali cycle in 2022 and 2023 remains the right operating mirror here. In a single year, falling spreads cut Olin’s fourth-quarter segment margin from 21.5% to 7.3%. Stallion’s own EBITDA margin fell from 17.7% to 6.9% once before, and Q2 FY27 proved how quickly core spreads still compress below 10%. When a management team keeps missing greenfield dates while dismissing cash conversion and equity-based compensation, investors must fail the scorecard rather than make excuses for it.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR’S REFLECTION
book_callouts.text: Write down the one date you care about most, and the day you will check it. If it slips once, note it. If it slips four times while management dismisses cash flow and ESOP dilution on an earnings call with no CFO present, stop giving the next promise the benefit of the doubt.
